prompt: Where did `history.py` get the stages of a job whose driver had already exited?

choices.text: The master's web page on port 8080
choices.why: The master lists applications, not stages.

choices.text: The executors, which keep their stages
choices.why: They do not keep a record.

choices.text: The history server, from the event log
choices.why: Right. The log was written as the job ran.

choices.text: The Parquet footers
choices.why: Footers describe files, not jobs.

prompt: A stage took 10 seconds of wall time and 30 seconds of task time. On average, how many tasks ran at once?
hint: Divide task time by wall time.

prompt: A stage has large task time, little input, no shuffle and no spill. What is it most likely doing?
hint: Nothing in the byte columns stands out.

choices.text: Waiting for a skewed partition in a join
choices.why: Skew shows in a shuffle-reading stage.

choices.text: Running out of memory
choices.why: That would show as spill or a failure.

choices.text: Writing a broadcast table
choices.why: A broadcast is small and quick.

choices.text: Slow work per row, such as a Python function
choices.why: Right. The time is in the rows, not the bytes.

prompt: Which single fix saved the most time in this lab?
hint: Look at the table's last column.

choices.text: Adaptive execution instead of 2,000 partitions
choices.why: Right: 57.4 seconds.

choices.text: A built-in function instead of Python
choices.why: 30.3 seconds.

choices.text: Parquet instead of CSV
choices.why: 25.4 seconds.

choices.text: Allowing the broadcast
choices.why: 2.1 seconds.

prompt: Why change one thing per run when tuning?
hint: What would four changes at once tell you?

choices.text: To keep the answer from changing
choices.why: None of the fixes changes the answer.

choices.text: To know which change mattered
choices.why: Right. The broadcast here saved two seconds.

choices.text: Each change needs its own cluster
choices.why: The same cluster ran all five.

choices.text: Spark rejects more than one new setting per run
choices.why: It accepts any number.

prompt: Why was DuckDB about twenty times faster than tuned Spark on this lab? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does Spark do that one process need not?

choices.text: No JVM and no executors to start
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: No shuffle between processes
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: It read different, smaller files
choices.why: It read the same silver files.

choices.text: It skipped the purchases filter
choices.why: Its totals matched Spark's exactly.

prompt: Why does `report_duckdb.py` read the timestamps through `timezone('UTC', ts)` before cutting them into months?
hint: What is stored in the files?

choices.text: DuckDB rounds timestamps to the hour
choices.why: It keeps them to the microsecond.

choices.text: Parquet stores dates as text
choices.why: Lesson 10: they are integers.

choices.text: DuckDB counts months from zero
choices.why: It counts them like everybody.

choices.text: They are instants in UTC, not local
choices.why: Right, and São Paulo's months begin three hours later than UTC's.

prompt: A cluster of 10 machines runs a 30-minute job once a day for 30 days, and exists only while the job runs. How many machine-hours is that?
What makes it possible to delete a cluster after each job without losing data?

choices.text: Spark caches the tables between jobs
choices.why: A cache dies with the application.

choices.text: HDFS replicates every block three times
choices.why: HDFS is on the cluster's own disks.

choices.text: The data lives in an object store
choices.why: Right. Nothing was on the cluster.

choices.text: Checkpoints are written to the driver
choices.why: And the driver goes with the cluster.

prompt: A notebook holds 4 executors for 8 hours and computes for 2 of them. At US$0.05 per executor-hour, how many dollars are spent on idle executors in that day?
Halving each executor's cores doubles the memory per task. What does it do to the cost of running 40 tasks at once?
hint: How many machines does it take?

choices.text: It doubles, because twice the machines are needed
choices.why: Right. A memory-optimised type is usually cheaper.

choices.text: It cannot be known without a run
choices.why: It is arithmetic: machines times price.

choices.text: It stays the same, because memory comes free with the cloud
choices.why: Memory comes with the machine you pay for.

choices.text: It halves, because each machine does less
choices.why: The work is the same; the machines are more.

prompt: Put lesson 7's fixes for spilling in the order to try them, cheapest first.
items: Fewer columns before the wide step

prompt: One task in two hundred spills. What does that call for?

choices.text: A different file format
choices.why: The format is not what spilled.

choices.text: Twice the memory on every executor
choices.why: That pays 200 times for one task.

choices.text: A fix for skew
choices.why: Right. Memory for every task would pay for one.

choices.text: Turning spilling off
choices.why: Then the task would fail instead.

prompt: When does a cluster earn its overhead? Choose all that apply.
hint: Past what one machine gets through in the time there is.

choices.text: A join of two tables too large for one machine
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A report of 120 rows from a small table
choices.why: Output size says nothing; input does.

choices.text: Terabytes to scan every night
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A 400 MB table read once a day
choices.why: DuckDB did that in a second.
